title: Before You Study: What Kind of Exhaustion Are You Feeling?

Mental.label: Mental Exhaustion
Mental.high: Your thinking system is the tired part right now — concentration, comprehension and problem-solving are all costing more effort than usual.
Mental.moderate: Some mental fatigue is showing. You can still study, but new and difficult material will feel heavier than it should.
Mental.low: Your thinking feels clear enough to take on new material.

Physical.label: Physical Exhaustion
Physical.high: Your body is asking for something — sleep, food, water, movement or rest. No study technique substitutes for that.
Physical.moderate: Your body is a little heavy. A short reset (water, a walk, a stretch) will probably buy you a usable study block.
Physical.low: Your body is not what's getting in the way right now.

Emotional.label: Emotional Exhaustion
Emotional.high: Something is draining your emotional energy. This is not laziness, and treating it as laziness will make the next hour worse, not better.
Emotional.moderate: There's some emotional drag. A very small, familiar task will start much more easily than a big one.
Emotional.low: Emotionally you have room to work.

Stress.label: Stress / Overload
Stress.high: Too much is being held in your head at once. The load itself — not the subject — is what's blocking you from starting.
Stress.moderate: Part of your attention is booked by things other than this study session.
Stress.low: Your head is reasonably clear of competing demands.

bands.label: Running On Empty
bands.text: Most of your systems are reporting tired at once. Forcing a long session now usually produces re-reading rather than learning.
bands.smallest: Recovery may genuinely be the more useful choice right now. If you must do something: 10 minutes of revising material you already know — nothing new.

bands.label: Noticeably Drained
bands.text: You have some capacity left, but not enough for your hardest chapter. Match the task to the tank.
bands.smallest: 10–15 minutes of revision or flashcards on something familiar. Stop when the timer stops — that counts as a finished session.

bands.label: Some Drag
bands.text: You're mostly functional with one or two things pulling at you. Clear those first and you'll get a good block out of today.
bands.smallest: A 25-minute active recall block — close the book and write down what you remember, then check.

bands.label: Good To Go
bands.text: Nothing is flagging strongly right now. This is the state to spend on your hardest material, not your easiest.
bands.smallest: Take on the difficult chapter or the problem set you've been avoiding. This is the energy you should be spending on it.

Mental.lead: Don't open the hardest new chapter first. Your thinking system needs to be warmed up, not thrown into deep water.
Mental.sequence: 10–15 minute reset → light recall → easy task → difficult task
do: Review material you have already learned
Flashcards or a quick self-quiz
Draw a mind map of a topic you know
Explain something you already understand, out loud
Organise or tidy your notes
A short retrieval-practice round
Mental.avoid: "Let me learn this completely new and difficult chapter right now."
Mental.rule: Reduce the cognitive load before you increase the difficulty.

Physical.lead: The useful question isn't "how do I force myself to study?" — it's "what does my body actually need?"
Physical.sequence: Meet the physical need → then re-check your energy → then choose the task
do: Check the obvious four: sleep, food, water, movement
Get out of the chair for five minutes
Fix the environment — light, air, a less collapsed posture
Take a genuine short rest instead of a scrolling break
Physical.avoid: Pushing through another hour while actually sleepy — the hour costs you the time and gives back almost no retention.
Physical.rule: If you are genuinely sleepy, sleep is the higher-value study decision.

Emotional.lead: Don't open with "I'm lazy." The accurate sentence is "something is draining my emotional energy" — and that's a solvable problem.
Emotional.sequence: Step away → name it → write it down → one small familiar task
do: Step away for a few minutes, properly
Identify what is actually bothering you
Write it down — out of your head, onto paper
Pick a very small study target
Start with something familiar, not something new
Give yourself permission to stop once that small target is done
Emotional.avoid: "I have to study chemistry for three hours." That target is what's keeping you from starting at all.
Emotional.rule: Swap the three-hour target for "I'll revise one concept for 15 minutes."

Stress.lead: Stress gets much harder to manage while everything is being held in your head at the same time. Get it out first.
Stress.sequence: Brain dump → sort → pick ONE task
do: Take a sheet of paper and write down everything that's worrying you
Sort each item: 🔴 must do today, 🟡 can do tomorrow, 🟢 can wait
Choose ONE thing from the red list
Start on that one thing only — the rest is now on paper, not in your head
Stress.avoid: Trying to study while mentally re-checking every deadline at once.
Stress.rule: Whatever is written down no longer needs to be remembered.

reflection: What is the smallest useful thing I can do right now?

steps: STOP — don't force yourself straight into it.
CHECK — which kind of exhaustion is this?
CHOOSE — what does my current state let me do well?
STUDY — pick the activity that fits.
closing.line: Don't always fight exhaustion. First understand it.

disclaimer: This is a self-reflection tool, not a medical or psychological diagnostic test. Persistent or severe fatigue, sleep problems, low mood, or difficulty functioning day to day should be discussed with a doctor or another appropriate healthcare professional.

questions.text: Am I finding it difficult to concentrate on one thing?
Am I reading the same sentence over and over without taking it in?
Is solving a simple problem taking much more effort than usual?
Does my mind feel overloaded with too many thoughts or too much information?
Does my body feel unusually tired or heavy?
Am I feeling sleepy, or struggling to keep my eyes open?
Do I feel I need food, water, movement or physical rest before I can study?
Does even sitting up and holding my posture feel tiring?
Do I feel emotionally drained even though my body isn't especially tired?
Am I unusually irritated, frustrated or easily upset?
Do I feel "I don't want to do anything" even when I have the energy to do it?
Does the idea of studying feel emotionally overwhelming right now?
Is my mind circling back to exams, deadlines, unfinished work or future problems?
Am I trying to study while worrying about several other things at the same time?
Do I feel heavy pressure that I "must study" without knowing where to start?
